title: Gbegiri from Canned Beans
author: Abidemi Olayiwola
desc: The thirty-minute gbegiri — canned beans blended with iru and half a cup of water, cooked covered, and total cooking time should not be more than twenty minutes.
longDesc: This is gbegiri with the two longest steps removed, and the author says so plainly: the recipe takes away the first two steps, which are the longest, so you only need to blend and cook. Canned haricot or black-eyed beans are drained, rinsed and blended with the locust beans and half a cup of water until smooth, then go into a saucepan with palm oil, ground prawns, pepper and salt, covered on reduced heat. Total cooking should not be more than twenty minutes. There is no peeling and no sieving — which is a real departure.
ingredients: 1 tsp pepper flakes or ground pepper powder
steps: Drain and rinse the beans in a colander.
Blend them with the locust beans and half a cup of water until smooth.
Pour into a saucepan with the palm oil, ground prawns, pepper and salt.
Total cooking time should not be more than 20 minutes.
chefTips: Twenty minutes maximum. The author states it directly and there is no benefit to longer — the beans are already cooked.
Blend the iru in with the beans rather than adding it to the pot. It disperses completely that way.
Rinse the canned beans properly. The canning liquid is salty and slightly metallic.
No peeling and no sieving here, which is the real departure. If the texture is too coarse for you, pass it through a sieve after blending — that is the one step worth adding back.
A tablespoon of palm oil for six servings makes this much lighter than the traditional versions, which use three tablespoons to a quarter cup.
Stir regularly. Blended beans catch on the base fast, and there is no long cooking stage to hide it.
This is a declared shortcut, not a traditional gbegiri. For the full version with soaking, peeling and sieving see NGA004.
commonMistakes: Cooking it for longer than twenty minutes.
Adding the iru whole to the pot.
Leaving it unstirred, so it catches.
Expecting the velvet texture of the peeled-and-sieved version.
sources: Adapted from 'How To Make Gbegiri Soup From Canned Beans', byline Abi Olayiwola, eatwellabi.com. Page metadata: prep 10 minutes, cook 20 minutes, servings 6.

Quantities exactly as printed: 1 can Haricot or black eye beans; 1 tablespoon Ground dried prawns; 1 teaspoon Fermented locust beans; 1 teaspoon Pepper flakes/ground pepper powder; 1 tablespoon Red palm-oil; 1 cube Bouillon; salt to taste. Plus the half cup of water from the method.

Method as printed: drain and rinse the beans in a colander; blend with the locust beans and '1/2 cup of water' until smooth; into a saucepan with palm oil, ground prawns, pepper and salt; cover, reduce heat; stir regularly; 'Total cooking time should not be more than 20 mins'; serve.

AUTHOR-FLAGGED DEVIATION, in her own words: 'This recipe takes away the first two steps which are the longest so you only need to blend and cook the soup.' Published as a declared shortcut rather than as traditional gbegiri.

WHAT IS MISSING RELATIVE TO THE TRADITIONAL VERSIONS, and it matters: there is NO PEELING STEP AT ALL — canned beans, skins unaddressed — and NO SIEVING STEP either, unlike Sisi Jemimah's version when hand-mashed and unlike Ajoke's, which sieves every time (NGA004, NGA005).

THIS IS ONE OF THE THREE POSITIONS ON THE GBEGIRI SKINS QUESTION, which was specifically investigated and is not reconciled: peeling is mandatory (Sisi Jemimah, and Tribune Online's Testimony Ishola); peeling is done but unpeeled beans are acceptable (Ajoke at My Active Kitchen, who says so explicitly); or peeling is skipped entirely via canned beans (here).

The palm oil is NOT bleached in any gbegiri version consulted — Ajoke is explicit that hers is heated about 3 minutes 'without bleaching oil'. Bleaching is an ayamase technique rather than a general palm-oil step, and that distinction holds across every gbegiri source.
reheating: Low heat with water to loosen. It sets firm cold.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas and haricot beans both supply plant protein, folate and soluble fibre.
Much lower in fat than the traditional versions at one tablespoon of oil for six servings.
Dried prawns add protein and iodine.
culturalNote: A thirty-minute gbegiri is not what anyone in Ibadan would make, and its author is honest that she has cut the two longest steps out. But it is the version a Nigerian cook abroad on a weeknight will actually produce, and knowing exactly which steps were removed — the soak and the peel — tells you what the long version is buying you.
